107.t: Hearing Charlie Parker and becoming a bebopper
107.s: In August 1945 hearing Parker made him a bebopper, though he later reappreciated Hodges, Smith and Carter.
107.q: Around August of 1945 I heard “Now is the Time” and “Billie’s Bounce” for the first time, and Charlie Parker for the first time. And from that moment forward, it was all over, I was a confirmed bebopper. And the idols that I had worshipped up to that time — Johnny Hodges, Willie Smith and Benny…

107.t: Analyzing Parker and Gillespie by ear
107.s: Foster and friends analyzed records, knew each note's function, and found bebop melodies more sophisticated than swing ones.
107.q: Yes, just not as aware of him as I was Bird and Diz, but I had some friends that really stayed on top of it as far as listening to records, collecting records. They kept me abreast of what was going on. As I said, when I heard Bird and Diz and Miles, I was fully drawn into this thing called bebop.…

107.s: Hearing Parker and Miles in 1945 made him a bopper; he describes the changes, extended chords and drummers 'dropping bombs'.
107.q: Up until that time it had been the swing thing. I was at a developmental stage of my life where whatever was going to be new at that time was bound to suck me in. When I first heard Charlie Parker and Miles Davis play Now’s the Time, and Billie’s Bounce, in the summer of 1945, that did it. I was a…

328.t: Hearing Things to Come: his brother and the record
328.s: The family discovered Dizzy Gillespie's Things to Come when the genius brother brought the record home.
328.ch: Carnegie Hall, bebop and the big bands
328.q: We had been hearing about Things to Come, and we were hoping we could find the recording. One day I was in a part of the house, and I heard this music start to play. They started playing. I knew, this has got to be Things to Come, because I haven’t heard any other music like that. [Hampton sings…

328.s: Hampton says the Montgomery brothers, Hubbard and J. J. Johnson led Indianapolis toward modern music.
328.ch: Carnegie Hall, bebop and the big bands
328.q: Yeah. We had already heard Charlie Parker and [Dizzy Gillespie’s] Things to Come in Indianapolis. That gave us our direction.

376.t: Abandoning mathematics for bebop and the 1949 Paris festival
376.s: Back in occupation-end Belgium he commits to music, studies Gillespie and Parker records, and becomes a bebopper before playing Paris in 1949.
376.ch: Bebop and the first American trip
376.q: Yes. Yes. And I’m… I played but we [inaudible]. I have to do [inaudible] for quite a few years. Play the melody for the people who want to dance so whatever, you know. And but I listened to all the records. I was totally acquainted, you know, the Dizzy Gillespie records and Charlie Parker, you…

376.t: When he visited and how he learned bebop
376.s: He places the trip in winter, and says he learned bebop vocabulary from records and on the spot.
376.ch: Bebop and the first American trip
376.q: It must, must have been… because… excuse me… the festival in Nice, where I had to join the Belgian delegation… [laughs] And that was… it must have been something like February or something.

129.t: Bound for Bermuda: seeing Lionel Hampton at Bop City and discovering vibes
129.s: On a flight stopover at Christmas 1949 he heard Hampton at Bop City; Hampton and Red Norvo's records had inspired him to play vibraphone.
129.ch: Vibes, Bermuda and arriving in Canada
129.q: Yes. We flew over on BOAC and we got behind. And consequently they put us up at the Gotham Hotel, 55th and Fifth Avenue. They don’t do that anymore. And I had never been to North America. All I could remember in my lifetime is rationing, you couldn’t buy clothes, couldn’t buy candies, you only got…

592.t: Parents' reaction to Parker, Dizzy and Konitz
592.s: His parents reacted to bebop as he did, first puzzled then open, and shared an open attitude toward jazz.
592.q: They reacted to it very much the same way we did. At first it was a little too much, you wondered what he was doing and that sort of thing. But over time they got used to that and so I couldn’t surprise them anymore. If I played something from somebody more remote, like Lee Konitz or someone, they…

131.t: First bebop record: Dizzy Gillespie's One Bass Hit
131.s: He hears One Bass Hit on 78 outside a music store in Oneonta in the early fifties.
131.q: The first bop record I ever heard was with my father when we went over to Oneonta, New York. In those days they used to have speakers outside of the music store playing the latest things, you know, that kind of thing. And we went in there, and I’ve still got the original 78. It was “One Bass Hit”…

324.t: First hearing Bird and Diz on furlough and learning bebop language
324.s: Gibbs heard Dizzy and Parker while on Army furlough, took Dizzy's syncopation, and after the Army learned bebop language, harmony and technique.
324.q: Well you’ve got to understand, when I first heard Bird and Diz I was home on furlough. And when I heard — I didn’t believe what I was hearing. But I know they were playing double-time, and I was in the Army by the way, I was on furlough. And in the Army I was the drummer with a 38-piece orchestra…

165.t: Hearing Salt Peanuts on the ship and buying bebop records
165.s: Heard Bird and Diz on the troopship radio, bought every bebop record, and turned Toledo musicians on.
165.q: We had this quick bandstand conversation. I had all his records when I came out of the Army. I had heard “Salt Peanuts” on the ship. I had won $300 shooting craps on the boat, and I heard this record from the ship’s radio room [scats]. I said whoa. Because it was in my head already from my Art…

593.t: Johnny Hodges and first hearing Charlie Parker
593.s: He grew up on Carter, Willie Smith and Hodges, then Coleman Hawkins told him to put on a Bird record and he heard the conception.
593.q: Yeah. I had grown up with Benny Carter, Willie Smith, I mean Johnny Hodges. I was so in awe of Hodges that one day he was coming out the back door, the stage door, of the RKO Theater in Boston. The Ellington band was there. I was so in awe I couldn’t even say hello. I mean that sound, that alto,…

441.t: Moving to Phoenix and converting to bop
441.s: The family moves to Phoenix in 1945; he joins the union, plays with Howard Roberts and shifts from swing to bop through Parker and Powell.
441.q: Why Phoenix? Well that crossed my mind too. I still hadn’t finished eighth grade yet, right? So my mother wanted to go out there for climatic reasons. And my dad during the war made a trip out as far as Tucson, because the trains were just packed with troops, it was hard — he worked at a defense…

576.t: Rebop, Charlie Parker and his Reboppers
576.s: Looking at plaques from Detroit, they discuss the early name rebop and the first record she bought.
576.q: That was the first record I ever bought was Charlie Parker and his Reboppers. Can I remember the label? Jeez I used to know but I can’t remember now. Yeah, Charlie Parker and his Reboppers. But shortly after that it went to bebop.

514.t: Hearing bebop through visiting big bands and friends' records
514.s: Radio rarely played Tatum, Parker or Powell, but Basie, Ellington and Hampton played the Palace Theater, and friends like George Coleman, Louis Smith and Phineas Newborn had the bebop records.
514.q: No, see that’s the thing. On the radio you didn’t hear no — first of all, on the radio you would hear maybe some Dave Brubeck and some George Shearing, but you didn’t really hear no Art Tatum, Charlie Parker, Bud Powell, at that time because that was too strong

159.t: First hearing bebop and joining the Harold Fox big band
159.s: A friend plays Charlie Parker Dial records; an anti-bebop bandleader dismisses the new style.
159.q: Yeah I remember the first time I heard it. It wasn’t on — was it on records or not? I think it was probably the same time — I was in high school, or I had just graduated from high school I think, or maybe during my last year of high school. I really was getting into it. And so there was a saxophone…

594.t: Hearing Charlie Parker and Jimmy Heath's compliment
594.s: He recalls the Parker 'linear logic' that made sense at 14-15, and reacts to Jimmy Heath's quote about his Parker language.
594.q: Yes. Right. That’s true. Yeah. And I think a lot of people felt that when they first heard Charlie Parker. I’m not the only one. But when I first heard Bird, yeah, that was overwhelming because it made perfect sense to me. And there was something about the way — because he played a lot of notes,…

595.t: Learning taste from Dizzy Gillespie and Charlie Parker
595.s: At 16 in Bob Astor's band, Pell played chess with Dizzy Gillespie in Boston, who took him to hear Parker and explained his thinking.
595.q: Taste is hard to acquire. You get taste from sitting next to great players and listening. I remember when I was real young, I mean 16 years old, I played in a band called Bob Astor, and my roommate was Neal Hefti. And the drummer in the band was Shelly Manne. And I remember going and playing in…

596.t: Bebop culture and the horn-rimmed glasses
596.s: Powell calls himself a bebop baby; he got horn-rimmed glasses and was mistaken for Mr. Tojo.
596.q: No it was a culture. Yeah it was, it was a whole lifestyle. So anyway I saw these horn rimmed glasses, so I had to have a pair of horn rimmed glasses. So I started squinting around and bumping into things and so forth. But my mother, she was hip to what I was doing, but she finally broke down and…

586.t: Charlie Parker tape and switching to stand-up bass
586.s: She loved a Parker tape without knowing who it was, moved from electric to upright bass in sophomore year, and won her first solo award.
586.q: I didn’t know who it was and I found out later, like the first one I had and listened to over and over again was Charlie Parker, Bird, you know, with the tune “Laura” and the strings and all of that. And I thought it was great but I didn’t know it was Charlie Parker. And so I was listening to that…

463.t: Bop, Parker, and Herbie Nichols as a bridge
463.s: He preferred swing at first, came to understand Parker and Monk later, and credits Herbie Nichols with opening him up around 1960-61.
463.q: I would have to say that from my own emotional understanding that the swing music say of Roy Eldridge, Coleman Hawkins and that kind of thing would have been sort of like the cutting edge for me, even though Bird and Monk and so forth were already out there changing things. When I heard Parker with…

597.t: Hearing Dizzy on Bird and Diz, and advice on unfamiliar music
597.s: First hearing of Dizzy Gillespie on Bird and Diz sounded foreign, leading to Artie Shaw's advice to listen 20 or 30 times.
597.q: You know and then of course I had other early influences. But those were very, very early. And those, now that I’m thinking about it and realizing it, those were the only two guys I heard very early that I was aware of. Those two guys. And then later I heard, I got to be a big Dizzy Gillespie fan.…

417.t: Bob Storey's trio, Larry Smith and first hearing Charlie Parker
417.s: Playing with organ trios in Pittsburgh, he forms his own group with saxophonist Larry Smith, who plays him Parker with strings (Just Friends).
417.ch: Teen bandleader and the road to McDuff
417.q: of Jimmy Smith and Johnny Smith and a few others, Wild Bill Davis and such. I was one of the few guys that played guitar. So they were all hitting on me. I ended up working in a group, the Bob Storey trio and then later the Bob Storey quartet. I kept hearing something I never heard before. We had a…

105.s: He first heard bebop live after the war, having only heard Bird's solo on a Jay McShann record, and a new crowd of players including Howard McGhee, Roy Porter and Sonny Criss.
105.ch: Bebop, band changes and the road
105.q: Jay McShann. There was a tenor player that used to play with him, T.J. Krump (?) was in the band, got drafted and they sent him there and he brought the record with him and Bird’s solo was on there and he used to tell us about Bird and that was it. That was it until I came home and heard all these…

142.t: His father introduces him to bebop with Charlie Parker LPs
142.s: His father played a Parker LP, Paquito did not like it, and his father insisted they learn it, bringing bebop books and records until they both loved it.
142.ch: Army, politics and jazz in Cuba
142.q: That’s a very good question. My father was a constant force in my life, you know; he was incredible. He came—I remember like today—he had a, one of those silver turntables. So he came with those little LPs, those small LPs, with the face of Charlie Parker, a very young Charlie Parker and that…

470.t: Cousin Walt's barbershop, bebop, Lester Young records and Dizzy Gillespie solos
470.s: He heard bebop all day at his cousin's barbershop, cousin Manson gave him Lester Young records, and his band mates learned Dizzy Gillespie heads.
470.ch: Crispus Attucks and the Indiana Avenue scene
470.q: This was Walt’s barbershop – and the swing stuff that led into bebop. He would play the music of Jay McShann and those guys. But then he also played the music of Charlie Parker and Dizzy Gillespie. We’re talking about now by 19 – this is by now 1945 or so. So I was hearing bebop all day long. I…

143.t: How Charlie Parker hit him and learning from McShann records
143.s: Parker's sound and drive changed everything; he slowed down worn McShann records to learn phrases.
143.q: Well, he was different. He was just different. The sound was different. The way he played was different, the way he would drive when he played, the power behind his phrases. Just different. And everything was swinging. Just different from anybody else. You actually would have to live back during…

104.t: Hearing Dizzy Gillespie's 'Hot House' at Charles Delaunay's in Paris
104.s: In Paris with the USO, Charles Delaunay played her 'Hot House' and she was baffled by the piano comping; she was aware of bebop but followed Jimmy's circle instead.
104.ch: Marriage, Chicago and arriving in New York
104.q: Oh yeah, certainly I was aware of Coleman Hawkins. Actually I’ll have to backtrack a little to when Jimmy and I were in Paris, before we’d come back here. We were still in U.S.O. We went to Charles Delaunay’s house. You know who . . .

233.s: Monk was getting turned on to bebop and Garner and Tatum, and local players were taking up the challenge.
233.q: : Jazz, babe, yeah. Well, by now, we listened to people like...Errol Garner was really in, and Art Tatum and in that era. Back in, oh, what year was this, like the middle forties, I guess. Late forties? A lot of good jazz. Bebop was in then, bebop was straight ahead.

170.t: Back in Chicago and hearing the "new music"
170.s: Ware had not worked in Chicago since the late thirties; he recalls hearing Bird with McShann and that nobody called it bebop.
170.q: Only at the end of my -- it was just before my discharge that I started hearing it, because we didn't hear it overseas. Not in Okinawa, anyway. I had heard a victory broadcast one night, but it wasn't reached over there. I didn't hear it until I got back to the States, and I just happened to hear a…
